lead: Above a certain power, silica stops being a passive pipe: the light itself drives two scattering processes. Stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) sends a frequency-shifted copy of the signal backward; stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) sends one mainly forward. Both take power from the signal, so each sets a ceiling on the power a fiber can carry. Only a few syllabi list these effects, and the exam asks for the mechanism, the threshold and the comparison. The same physics is used on purpose in Brillouin sensors and Raman amplifiers.
prereq: You need: the attenuation coefficient in dB/km and nepers from attenuation, and linear Rayleigh scattering.

blocks.text: Rayleigh scattering is linear and elastic: the scattered light has the signal’s frequency and its share does not depend on power. The nonlinear kinds are inelastic: the scattered photon, called the Stokes wave, has less energy than the signal photon, and the difference goes into the glass. Below threshold this happens spontaneously and weakly. Above threshold the Stokes wave grows exponentially, fed by the signal.

SBS. The signal and the backward Stokes wave beat together, and their interference pattern compresses the glass by electrostriction, driving an acoustic wave. That acoustic wave is a moving index grating which reflects more signal backward, Doppler-shifted down by νB = 2nvA/λ, where vA ≈ 5960 m/s is the speed of sound in silica. At 1550 nm this is about 11 GHz. The Brillouin gain band is only about 20 to 50 MHz wide, so a narrow-line laser puts all its power inside it and reaches threshold at a few milliwatts.

SRS. The signal scatters off molecular vibrations of silica (optical phonons). The Stokes wave is shifted down by about 13 THz, roughly 100 nm at 1550 nm, and travels in both directions, the forward wave growing along with the signal. The Raman gain band is very wide, about 40 THz, and the gain coefficient is small, so the threshold is hundreds of milliwatts.
Only the first part of a span is bright enough to drive these effects, because the signal fades along the fiber. The effective length counts that part:

blocks.where: L<sub>eff</sub> is the effective length in m; α is the attenuation coefficient in nepers per metre (dB/km ÷ 4343); L is the physical length in m. For a long span L<sub>eff</sub> → 1/α, about 21.7 km at 0.2 dB/km.

blocks.text: The threshold is the launch power at which the Stokes wave grows as large as the signal at the output. For a narrow-line source the usual estimates are

Pth,B ≈ 21 Aeff/(gBLeff)
Pth,B is the SBS threshold in W; Aeff is the effective core area in m²; gB ≈ 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m/W is the peak Brillouin gain coefficient.

Pth,R ≈ 16 Aeff/(gRLeff)
Pth,R is the SRS threshold in W; gR ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁴ m/W is the peak Raman gain coefficient near 1550 nm.

Many textbooks also give empirical forms in practical units, with d the core diameter in µm, λ in µm, α<sub>dB</sub> in dB/km and ν the source bandwidth in GHz: P<sub>B</sub> = 4.4 × 10⁻³ d²λ²α<sub>dB</sub>ν watts and P<sub>R</sub> = 5.9 × 10⁻² d²λα<sub>dB</sub> watts. The Brillouin form is for a source much wider than the Brillouin band, so it grows with ν; widening the source spreads its power over many Brillouin bands.

items: SBS caps the power per channel. Above threshold extra launch power is reflected back toward the transmitter, adding noise. Cures: stay below threshold, or dither the laser to widen its spectrum beyond the Brillouin band.
SRS acts on the whole WDM band. Short-wavelength channels pump long-wavelength ones, so the spectrum tilts; the limit is on the total launched power.
Used on purpose: Brillouin sensors read strain and temperature along a fiber from shifts of ν<sub>B</sub>, and Raman amplifiers pump the transmission fiber about 13 THz above the signal.

examples.question: An 80 km span at 1550 nm has α = 0.2 dB/km and A<sub>eff</sub> = 80 µm². Take g<sub>B</sub> = 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m/W and g<sub>R</sub> = 7 × 10⁻¹⁴ m/W. (a) Find L<sub>eff</sub>. (b) Find the SBS and SRS thresholds for a narrow-line source. (c) A 40-channel WDM system launches 4 mW per channel; comment.
steps: L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − 0.0251) ÷ 4.605 × 10⁻⁵ = 21 170 m = 21.2 km, close to the limit 1/α = 21.7 km.

(c) Each channel at 4 mW is above the 1.6 mW SBS threshold, so the lasers must be dithered. The total 40 × 4 = 160 mW is below the 0.86 W single-channel SRS threshold, but across a wide WDM band Raman tilt becomes noticeable at total powers of this order, so the edge channels need gain equalisation.
examples.answer: L<sub>eff</sub> = 21.2 km; P<sub>th,B</sub> ≈ 1.6 mW and P<sub>th,R</sub> ≈ 0.86 W; the link is limited per channel by SBS.

examples.question: Using the empirical formulas, compare the SBS and SRS thresholds for a single-mode fiber with core diameter 8 µm and loss 0.2 dB/km at 1.55 µm, driven by a source of 0.5 GHz bandwidth. Repeat at 1.31 µm, where the loss is 0.35 dB/km.
examples.answer: About 68 mW for SBS and 1.2 W for SRS at 1.55 µm, and 85 mW and 1.7 W at 1.31 µm. The 0.5 GHz source raises the SBS threshold far above the narrow-line 1.6 mW of the first example, but SBS still comes first.

traps: Using the physical length where the formula needs L<sub>eff</sub>. An 80 km span at 0.2 dB/km acts like 21.2 km.
Converting dB/km to nepers per metre wrongly. Divide by 4.343 for Np/km, and by 4343 for Np/m.
Swapping the two: Brillouin is backward, about 11 GHz, a band of tens of MHz; Raman is about 13 THz, a band of tens of THz.
Converting A<sub>eff</sub> wrongly: 80 µm² is 80 × 10⁻¹² m², not 80 × 10⁻⁶ m².
Saying SRS limits each channel separately. Its wide band couples all channels, so it limits the total power.

quiz.q: Which stimulated scattering is backward, and what are the two frequency shifts at 1550 nm?
quiz.a: SBS is backward with about 11 GHz shift; SRS has about 13 THz shift and grows mainly forward.

quiz.q: Why does the threshold formula use L<sub>eff</sub> instead of L?
quiz.a: The signal decays along the span, so only roughly the first 1/α of the fiber is bright enough to drive the effect; more length adds almost nothing.

quiz.q: Find ν<sub>B</sub> at 1310 nm with n = 1.45 and v<sub>A</sub> = 5960 m/s.
A span has A<sub>eff</sub> = 50 µm², g<sub>B</sub> = 5 × 10⁻¹¹ m/W and L<sub>eff</sub> = 21.2 km. Find the SBS threshold.
Give the order of magnitude of the SBS and SRS thresholds for a narrow-line source at 1550 nm.
quiz.a: A few mW for SBS; hundreds of mW to about 1 W for SRS.

quiz.q: Why does SBS limit the power per channel while SRS limits the total power?
quiz.a: The Brillouin band is tens of MHz, narrower than one channel, so each channel acts alone. The Raman band is tens of THz and covers the whole WDM band, so the channels pump one another.

quiz.q: Why does dithering the laser raise the SBS threshold but not the SRS threshold?
quiz.a: Dithering spreads the power over GHz, far wider than the Brillouin band, so little power drives any one acoustic wave. The Raman band is so wide that the dithered line still sits inside it.

beyond: Brillouin optical time-domain analysis (BOTDA) turns a whole fiber into a strain and temperature sensor for pipelines, dams and bridges. Distributed Raman amplifiers pump the transmission fiber itself, and Raman fiber lasers use cascaded Stokes shifts to reach new wavelengths. High-power fiber lasers fight SBS with large-mode-area fibers. Search for “BOTDA sensor”, “distributed Raman amplification” and “SBS suppression phase dithering”.

figure.caption: The signal fades along the 80 km span, so only the first part drives nonlinear scattering: the dashed rectangle of the same area is the effective length, 21.2 km. Above it, the Raman Stokes wave runs forward and the Brillouin Stokes wave runs back toward the transmitter.

spec.aria: Graph of signal power falling exponentially along an 80 kilometre span, with a dashed rectangle 21.2 kilometres wide of equal area marking the effective length; above the graph a forward arrow for Raman scattering and a dashed backward arrow for Brillouin scattering.
